history.new: Verified for n = 5..16 and for the products 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 56, 63, 72; sampling hit rates (close to 1/n^2 per random Latin square) suggest the number of full-period quasigroups of order n grows like L(n)/n^2 (L(n) = number of Latin squares), but there is no proof. Lexicographic DFS (3e6 nodes) and SAT (3e5 conflicts) fail from n = 9 on, random sampling succeeds (EXP-C16-05).
history.old: Verified for n = 5..16 and for the products 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 56, 63, 72; sampling hit rates (about 1/n^2 per random Latin square of the right parity) suggest the number of full-period quasigroups grows like L(n)/n^2, but there is no proof. Plain depth-first search and a SAT encoding stall at n = 9, so random sampling was the only method that scaled.

history.new: Verified for n = 5..16 and for the products 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 56, 63, 72; the Skeptic's own sampler adds verified examples for every n = 17..26 and full-period Z_n-isotopes for odd n <= 21. Sampling hit rates are of the order 1/n^2 per random Latin square but not close to it (exact n = 5 rate 0.52/n^2; pooled over n = 6..16 the lab has 139 hits against 181 expected), so a count of order L(n)/n^2 (L(n) = number of Latin squares) is suggested, without proof. Lexicographic DFS (3e6 nodes) and SAT (3e5 conflicts) fail from n = 9 on, random sampling succeeds (EXP-C16-05).

statement: For every n >= 5 there is a quasigroup of order n whose Fibonacci pair map is a single cycle through all n^2 pairs.
title: Full-period quasigroups exist for every order n >= 5
